sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
September 2026 delivered one of the most bifurcated global equity tapes of the current cycle. U.S. mega-cap technology and AI-levered growth names drove the Nasdaq Composite to a fresh record intraday high of **27,244.28** on September 22 even as the Federal Reserve resumed rate hikes, while value-oriented and rate-sensitive benchmarks — most notably the Dow Jones Industrial Average — bore the brunt of a Treasury yield surge that pushed the 10-year to **5.29%**, near its highest level since 2007. The MSCI World Index declined an estimated **-1.2%** in U.S. dollar terms (approx., verify before merging), though it retained a robust year-to-date gain of roughly **+12%** (approx., verify before merging), underscoring the enduring resilience of risk assets against renewed monetary tightening.

The month's defining tension was the collision between powerful corporate earnings momentum — S&P 500 second-quarter profits rose **+52%** year-on-year with an **86%** beat rate — and a macro backdrop darkened by the Fed's first rate hike in over three years, a Middle East energy shock that pushed Brent crude to an intraday peak of **$131/barrel**, and synchronised tightening from the ECB and BoJ within the same calendar fortnight. The net result was a market that rewarded AI-exposed large caps and punished rate-sensitive, energy-importing sectors in equal measure, producing some of the widest intra-index dispersion of 2026.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes:
Fed's First Rate Hike in Three Years Resets the Policy Landscape -- On September 16, the Federal Open Market Committee unanimously raised the federal funds target range by **25 basis points** to **3.75%–4.00%** — the first Fed rate increase since 2023 and a decisive end to five consecutive hold decisions. The updated Summary of Economic Projections lifted the median 2026 rate dot to **4.1%**, signalling one further hike by year-end, while the 2026 core PCE forecast was revised to **3.4%**, reflecting the persistence of above-target inflation compounded by the energy shock from the U.S.-Iran conflict.

The rate decision catalysed a sharp repricing across the Treasury curve: the 10-year yield climbed to **5.29%** by September 30 — approaching levels last seen in 2007 — while the 2-year settled at **4.88%**, widening the 2s10s spread to a positive **+41 basis points** in a tentative bear steepening. Broad investment-grade credit fell approximately **-2.7%** for the month, among its weakest performances in four years, and rate-sensitive equity sectors including real estate, utilities, and small caps bore disproportionate damage, with the Russell 2000 estimated to have declined nearly **-6%** (approx., verify before merging).

Middle East Escalation Triggers Historic Oil Price Spike -- The U.S.-Iran conflict entered a dramatically more acute phase in September, with coordinated strikes on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline driving Brent crude to an intraday peak of **$131/barrel** on September 15 — a level the IEA characterised as the highest since the conflict's escalation phase began. The EIA estimated the monthly average Brent spot price at approximately **$114/barrel** for September (EIA estimate, approx., verify before merging), some **$23/barrel** above August's average, as geopolitical risk premiums were aggressively priced back into global energy markets following months of relative calm.

Brent crude ended the month near **$98/barrel** (approx., verify before merging) as emergency strategic reserve releases from IEA member nations and diplomatic signals of a partial supply corridor agreement trimmed the extreme risk premium, though the level remained materially above August's close. WTI settled near **$90/barrel** (approx., verify before merging) by month-end. The energy shock materially complicated every major central bank's inflation calculus simultaneously — adding a supply-side inflationary impulse at precisely the moment policymakers were attempting to cool demand-driven price pressures — while widening the performance gap between energy-exporting and energy-importing economies.

AI Mega-Cap Concentration Defies the Rate Headwind -- The Nasdaq Composite gained approximately **+1.7%** in September to close near **26,861**, with the Nasdaq-100 outperforming at an estimated **+3.3%** (approx., verify before merging), as concentrated institutional flows into AI-exposed mega-caps proved durable enough to absorb a concurrent surge in risk-free discount rates. The index briefly reached a record closing high of **27,244.28** on September 22 — a remarkable achievement given the 10-year Treasury yield's simultaneous climb toward **5.29%** — reflecting the market's willingness to assign premium multiples to businesses seen as structural AI infrastructure beneficiaries.

The dynamic produced a dangerously narrow market beneath the surface. The S&P 500's modest **-0.7%** monthly decline masked far weaker performance from equal-weighted indices and small caps, and technology and communications services were the only S&P 500 sectors to record positive returns for September. The bifurcation reinforces a central 2026 equity market debate: whether AI-driven earnings power is sufficiently durable to sustain current valuations as the risk-free rate approaches **5.3%**, or whether multiple compression is simply being deferred rather than avoided.

Synchronised G3 Central Bank Tightening — A Rare Macro Event -- September 2026 produced an unusual and potentially consequential macro configuration: the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank, and the Bank of Japan each tightened monetary policy within the same calendar month, creating the first synchronised G3 tightening episode in recent memory. The ECB raised its deposit rate by **25 basis points** to **2.50%** on September 10, citing a three-year high in euro-area inflation, and the BoJ lifted its policy rate to **1.25%** on a 7–2 vote on September 18, continuing its landmark normalisation from decades of ultra-loose policy. The Bank of England broke the G3 pattern, holding its Bank Rate at **3.75%** on a 6–3 vote on September 17, though three dissenters pushing for an immediate hike signal that further BoE tightening remains live.

The collective effect of simultaneous policy action across the world's three largest reserve currency issuers reverberated through global asset prices: the DXY rose approximately **+2.4%** to near **101.0** (approx., verify before merging) as U.S. rate differentials and safe-haven demand converged, emerging-market currencies faced broad pressure as dollar-denominated debt burdens increased, and duration assets globally posted their largest single-month drawdown of 2026. For cross-asset strategists, the synchronised tightening moment marks a potential inflection: if all three central banks continue hiking simultaneously into Q4, the cumulative drag on global growth could prove more severe than any individual rate cycle.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
U.S. equities posted a divergent September tape: the S&P 500 declined **-0.7%** to close at **7,651.54**, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell approximately **-4.9%** to **50,908** (approx., verify before merging) — its worst monthly performance of 2026 — while the Nasdaq Composite bucked the trend with a **+1.7%** gain to roughly **26,861**. The Nasdaq-100 outperformed the broader market at an estimated **+3.3%** (approx., verify before merging), buoyed by concentrated buying in AI-facing large caps even as the 10-year Treasury yield surged toward multi-decade highs. The Nasdaq set a fresh record closing high of **27,244.28** on September 22.

Sector dispersion was extreme and revealing. Technology and communications services were the only S&P 500 sectors to record positive monthly returns, as AI enthusiasm sustained elevated multiples for mega-caps whose forward earnings estimates continued to grind higher. Rate-sensitive sectors — real estate, utilities, consumer staples, and financials — led declines as the 10-year yield's rise to **5.29%** increased discount rates and pressured dividend-paying names. Small-cap indices declined an estimated **-6%** (approx., verify before merging) as higher borrowing costs disproportionately weighed on balance sheets more dependent on floating-rate debt.

The S&P 500's Q2 earnings season, which concluded mid-month, provided a fundamental anchor: profits grew **+52%** year-on-year with an **86%** beat rate, supporting the bull case that corporate earnings power remains intact. However, forward guidance was cautious around energy cost pass-through, particularly for consumer-facing and industrial names. The Fed's unanimous September 16 hike to **3.75%–4.00%**, with the dot plot signalling a terminal **4.1%** rate for 2026, sets the stage for continued rate sensitivity in equity valuations heading into Q4.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equity markets navigated a challenging September shaped by two compounding headwinds: the ECB's return to active tightening and a surge in energy import costs from the Persian Gulf. The FTSE 100 closed the month at approximately **10,606** (approx., verify before merging), the DAX settled near **25,104** (approx., verify before merging), and the CAC 40 ended around **7,769** (approx., verify before merging). The region's structural dependence on imported hydrocarbons amplified the oil-price shock relative to North American peers, compressing margins for energy-intensive industrials and squeezing household disposable income.

The European Central Bank's September 10 decision to raise its deposit rate by **25 basis points** to **2.50%** — its second increase of 2026 — came as euro-area headline inflation surged to a three-year high, driven in part by the energy shock. EUR/USD slid from approximately **1.16** at the start of the month to near **1.1403** by late September (approx., verify before merging), reflecting both the Fed's relatively more aggressive tightening pace and the net negative terms-of-trade shock facing the eurozone from elevated oil import bills. ECB officials signalled that further tightening remains conditional on the inflation trajectory, leaving markets uncertain about the Q4 path.

Defensive and energy-sector names provided partial offsets across European indices, but the broader European picture was one of compressed margin expectations, slowing export demand toward China, and growing concern that the ECB's tightening cycle could overshoot into a policy error given the simultaneous external energy shock. Peripheral sovereign credit spreads widened modestly as higher global yields pressured weaker eurozone credits — a channel that investors will monitor closely should the ECB continue hiking into a softening growth environment.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Japanese equities demonstrated notable resilience in September, with the Nikkei 225 closing at approximately **66,754** for an estimated **+0.7%** monthly gain (approx., verify before merging), a solid outcome given the Bank of Japan's September 18 decision to raise its policy rate to **1.25%** on a 7–2 vote. The BoJ hike — the highest policy rate since 1995 — was interpreted constructively by the market as a validation of Japan's genuine wage and economic growth momentum rather than destabilising tightening. Bank and financial sector stocks rallied on the rate increase, helping to offset pressure on export-oriented manufacturers from meaningful yen appreciation. The Nikkei remains well below its June record near **73,600** but held its year-to-date advance of approximately **+29%** (approx., verify before merging).

The USD/JPY cross fell from approximately **160** at the start of September to near **154** by month-end (approx., verify before merging), a yen appreciation of approximately **-3.7%** against the dollar, driven by the BoJ hike combined with elevated intervention expectations. While a stronger yen weighs on reported earnings for Japan's globally-oriented corporate sector, real-money investors increasingly view BoJ normalisation as a structural positive — signalling that Japanese assets can attract capital without the explicit backstop of ultra-loose monetary accommodation. The index is digesting whether rising domestic real rates will constrain further multiple expansion.

China's equity markets faced distinct and compounding pressures. The Hang Seng traded near **24,211** (approx., verify before merging) and the Shanghai Composite near **3,813** (approx., verify before merging), as surging oil import costs, a stronger dollar tightening EM financial conditions, persistent deflationary domestic pressures, and geopolitical uncertainty capped a recovery that had shown early-month promise. The PBOC's accommodative policy stance — in stark contrast to G3 peers tightening simultaneously — creates an unusual divergence in global monetary policy that has implications for EM capital flows and Chinese asset valuations into year-end.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The U.S. dollar strengthened broadly in September, with the DXY rising approximately **+2.4%** to close near **101.0** (approx., verify before merging) as the Fed's **25 basis point** hike to **3.75%–4.00%** on September 16, the resulting surge in U.S. real yields, and safe-haven demand from the escalating Middle East conflict converged simultaneously. The advance was broad-based across most major currency pairs, with the Japanese yen as the notable exception. EUR/USD fell from approximately **1.16** at the start of September to near **1.1403** by late September (approx., verify before merging), as the ECB's deposit rate of **2.50%** remained materially below the Fed's policy rate, and the eurozone's terms-of-trade deterioration from the oil shock weighed on the single currency.

GBP/USD declined from approximately **1.35** to near **1.3252** by late September (approx., verify before merging) as the Bank of England held its Bank Rate at **3.75%** on September 17 — a cautious pause in contrast to its G3 peers' active tightening — leaving sterling poorly positioned against a resurgent dollar. The three BoE dissenters voting for an immediate hike suggest the Monetary Policy Committee may resume tightening in Q4, providing a partial GBP floor. EUR/GBP remained relatively range-bound as both currencies faced similar dollar headwinds.

USD/JPY's move was September's standout in G10 FX: the pair fell from approximately **160** to near **154** (approx., verify before merging), a dollar decline of approximately **-3.7%**, as the BoJ's hike to **1.25%** combined with sustained intervention expectations drove substantial yen appreciation. The move represents a meaningful unwind of yen carry positions accumulated through the earlier 2026 weaker-yen period, with real-money and macro accounts cutting short-yen exposure ahead of anticipated further BoJ normalisation. The divergence between a strengthening yen and broadly firming dollar against other G10 peers reflects the BoJ's increasingly distinctive policy trajectory.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Energy markets dominated the commodity complex in September, with the U.S.-Iran conflict producing one of the most acute intra-month oil price shocks in recent years. Brent crude surged to an intraday peak of **$131/barrel** on September 15 following attacks on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, before partially reversing as emergency IEA strategic reserve releases and diplomatic signals of a partial supply corridor agreement trimmed the extreme geopolitical risk premium. The EIA estimated the September monthly average Brent spot price at approximately **$114/barrel** (EIA estimate, approx., verify before merging), some **$23/barrel** above August's average. Brent ended the month near **$98/barrel** (approx., verify before merging) and WTI settled near **$90/barrel** (approx., verify before merging), with the Brent-WTI spread elevated by Middle Eastern supply disruption risks.

Gold was a notable underperformer despite the geopolitical backdrop, falling approximately **-6%** for the month (Janus Henderson estimate, approx., verify before merging) from above **$4,400/oz** to near **$4,220/oz** (approx., verify before merging). The yellow metal's weakness reflected the dominant force of rising real yields: as nominal Treasury yields surged to **5.29%** and long-run inflation expectations remained broadly anchored, gold's opportunity cost increased materially. The metal's inability to sustain safe-haven gains — despite a genuine geopolitical shock — highlights the asymmetric sensitivity of gold to the discount rate environment at current valuation levels. Copper gained approximately **+1%** to near **$6.71/lb** (approx., verify before merging), supported by the AI infrastructure investment theme — data centre construction remains a meaningful copper demand driver — though broader gains were capped by Chinese industrial demand uncertainty.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
September 2026 was the worst month for core fixed income in several years, as the Fed's resumption of rate hikes and the energy-driven inflation shock catalysed a sustained sell-off across the Treasury curve. The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield rose to **5.29%** by September 30 — approaching levels not seen since 2007 — from an estimated **4.73%** at end-August (approx., verify before merging), a move of approximately **+56 basis points**. The 2-year yield settled at **4.88%**, with the resulting **+41 basis point** positively sloped 2s10s spread representing a tentative bear steepening consistent with markets beginning to price higher long-run neutral rates alongside near-term tightening. The broad U.S. investment-grade bond index declined approximately **-2.7%** for the month, among its weakest monthly performances in four years.

The velocity and breadth of the Treasury sell-off reflected three concurrent drivers: the FOMC's unanimous September 16 hike to **3.75%–4.00%** accompanied by a dot plot projecting the terminal 2026 rate at **4.1%**, the inflationary signal from oil reaching **$131/barrel** intra-month, and growing investor concern over U.S. fiscal sustainability requiring structurally higher term premia. The combination has reintroduced bond vigilante dynamics for the first time since the 2022–2023 cycle. The distinction between a cyclical rates overshoot and a secular shift in the neutral rate is becoming an increasingly live debate among fixed income strategists, with the 10-year's continued climb toward and potentially through **5.3%** serving as the test case.

Globally, developed market government bonds sold off in sympathy: UK Gilt yields rose materially as markets recalibrated BoE tightening expectations, German Bund yields tested levels that raised questions about ECB credibility, and peripheral eurozone spreads — Italian BTPs versus German Bunds in particular — widened modestly as higher global rates pressured weaker sovereign credits. High-yield credit spreads widened an estimated **+25–35 basis points** (approx., verify before merging) in sympathy with the small-cap equity rout. TIPS underperformed nominal Treasuries as inflation breakevens compressed despite the oil shock, suggesting the market views the energy effect as temporary — a judgement that will be tested against October's CPI print.
